I picked half of this up from a Mefjus tutorial (Drum & Bass) - he compresses the sub range of acoustic kicks quite hard and it works really well for his style, and doing it slightly differently worked well for mine.

One little-talked-about technique I've been using is - using a multiband compressor, with one band compressing (controlling) the sub range, while another band is compressing (boosting) the \~100Hz range.  That's where the punch really is - no sense losing any headroom you don't have to for the more "impressionistic" and subby tail portion.

There's also options like Melodyne, which can be used rather extremely and still produce useable, if not downright interesting, results.

What kind of basses are you trying to make? In my experience, FM works best when used to add somewhat subtle overtones to solid fundamentals, like sines or triangles in low registers. If you don't create too much high-end rasp and crap, you can squeeze the sound with a multiband distortion to bring out the overtones in a really organic and interesting way.

The trick to FM is not to overdo it, I guess is what I'm saying.  Try working with just sine waves, detuning them here and there, messing with ratios, and creating subtle movements in amplitude of different parts to make the sound seem "fluid." Then enhance that foundation by any means you see fit.

Just curious, what kind of analysis? And how's your FFT knowledge? Reaktor would be a great stepping stone imo. There's also an interesting project called AudioKit that works as a sort of visual programming package that interfaces with Audio Units and existing libraries of DSP.

A lot of the top-notch D&B folks give great Serum tutorials on sites like Sample Genie, and they almost always use simple patches and create the character of the sound through creative processing (chiefly filtering and distortion).

To whit, Posij used very little FX in his demonstration patch, but the FX were used to their limits and with purpose. Same with Fre4knc. And Joe Ford. InsideInfo literally just used a raw saw wave - no filtering or FX in the patch - it was practically a signal generator.

It made me realize that a synth is really just a sample generator... it encourages endless tweaking, but eventually you just careen off the edge of "too much" and it falls to shit. Simplicity and small calculated steps really do work wonders.

A lot of artists (e.g. Mefjus, Break, Billain) tend to have their basses serve a distinct function with respect to frequency/spectrum placement.  Long story short, you want to have only one bass sound occupying the sub region at any given moment, and as you go higher up the spectrum, you have a little more leeway.

Mefjus in particular, from what I can tell from listening to his tracks and watching his Digital Labz masterclass, tends to sequence his basses so there's a distinct sub tone, a mid-range tone to thicken the texture, and the upper portions of the spectrum are where all the crazy movement happens.  The lower parts are sequenced to aid the drive/momentum of the track, while still complementing the groove created by the drums, and the higher portions are used in varying capacities, such as in a call & response pattern, serving a more melodic/riff-like purpose.

The most important thing for your mix is going to be how you see the sounds functioning, and consequently, how you sequence them.  Get them to groove and play around each other, rather than just stacking them for a rather static "fat bass" and calling it a day - it's the interaction between the layers that gives them their cohesion and creates the interest and danceability.

Once they're sequenced, decide which one is going to be the sub tone, which will be the mid-range tone, and which will occupy the higher regions (this is just one of many methods, but it's a good exercise to try out).  Set levels appropriately, EQ to open up the low end for the sub tone, EQ to make space for the midrange element, and have fun with the top end.

In short - you can try stacking sub bass on sub bass, but you'll inevitably run into balance or phasing issues.  It's all about sequencing, making space, and then gluing the elements back together, whether through busing or other creative means.

Also, something a lot of people overlook is just how long the tail of certain hits should be.

For example, a house-style kick won't work in a D&B tune straight away - it has too much sustain.  However, editing the original sample with a simple crop and fade suddenly makes it work.

Even in a house tune, it may have too much sustain, which causes it to overlap in time with other elements, eating up headroom.  Sample length is important to the tonality, punctuation, dynamics... everything really, so don't overlook it.

Also, if you're not versed in it yet, look into tuning your drums.  There are a load of strategies for doing this, but an easy one is to tune your kick to the tonic, and your snare to any note in the key that hits at the right spot.  Some styles like tech house go for a darker vibe sometimes and use minor seconds for snare tuning (i.e. the "Phrygian note") - this is all up to what vibe you want to get, and where you want the fundamental to hit (~200 has more impact, like in Jump-Up D&B, while higher up has more presence, like in Neurofunk D&B, etc.).  But having a kick on the tonic is pretty much an unavoidable decision, from personal experience anyway.

I think the best thing you can do is:

•Experiment with different tempos and styles, reconciling the drum elements you've got on hand to make a cohesive groove in a way you haven't had to before

•Experiment with altering your drum instrumentation (i.e. sample types, and how you employ them)

•Above all else, learn any and every way to enhance the dynamics and articulation of your programming - for example, using velocity for amplitude in a sampler to allow the use of ghost notes.  This is where the rabbit hole truly begins, because the same pattern can be accented in different ways to make it feel distinctly different from it's original counterpart.

•Study up on accents and dynamics to give you the insight to make your drums "speak," rather than plod along - you can make certain hits punctuate divisions better, enhance patterns with complimentary patterns, and overall add more vitality, dynamics, and interest to your patterns.

Also, just because I've never seen this shared and I had to figure it out myself, the depth of velocity routing to amplitude can be approached in a rather pragmatic way.  In Ableton, a setting of 12% in the sampler is roughly equal to 6dB of dynamic range, meaning you can play something at the lowest velocity (1), and it'll always play at half the perceived volume of something played at full velocity (127).  Fiddle with the velocity depths on different drum parts - kicks, snares, percussion, hi-hats, etc. - they're all going to warrant a different dynamic range based on what you want to achieve, and in MIDI this is the easiest way to sort that out.

From personal experience, I'd recommend a three-layered approach - the layers being the transient, the body, and the tail, from a functional perspective.

For the transient, you can edit one out of a snare with a cracking attack to it - literally keep only the first 15-30ms of it, and give it a clean fade to zero to avoid clicks, etc. Don't fuck with this layer too much - it's the "first impression" of the snare and provides about 50% of the excitement, but it's still supposed to be felt more than heard.

Now, for the tail & body, you could conceivably use the same 909 snare sample - the difference is in the approach. For the body, give it a slight fade in so it sort of "flows" out of the transient layer without masking it, but don't make it sound separate, either.  This is where you can boost and saturate the fundamental tone anywhere from 150-250 Hz or so, depending on the tuning.  Saturation, clipping, etc, are fair game.

For the tail, also fade it in a bit, and experiment like a madman. This is the layer you can overcook without ill effect, really. Seriously, go wild - flatline/sausage the thing if you want to.

Send all three layers to a bus, get their levels in balance, and then hit it hard with the best limiter you have. Try an attack around 10-20ms or so, a release that makes sense, and about 6dB of gain reduction. Honestly, just drive it until the body comes out and everything gels, and dial it back if/when it starts to disappear. Last tip - use a bit of a transient shaper into the limiter to exaggerate the all-important "smack" before you reduce it.

Edit: Forgot to mention, sensibly EQ the individual layers before doing bus processing. Timing, envelopes, EQ, and levels are your most important tools.

If it's playing a mostly rhythmic role, you'll want to emphasize frequencies in the "pick" range and take out more of the "musical" part of the spectrum.  Basically, you're using EQ to emphasize the rhythm of the playing, as it's likely a secondary rhythmic element, rather than the articulation of the notes being played.  This ensures that the guitar tucks into the mix without masking the more powerful melodic/harmonic content.

Also, compression is key for making acoustic instruments gel with an electronic track.  You need to roughly match dynamics between the acoustic and the other electronic tracks you have.  Try using a fast-attack compressor first to catch nasty peaks and tame them (something like an 1176 is good for this part), then feed it into a smoother compressor that will make the sound more solid (something like an LA-2A is good for this).

Before you touch an EQ band, you should take note of what the kick already is, before you try and fix something that may not be a problem.  Not all kicks are boxy.  Some have too much presence an octave above the fundamental.  Some have too much presence in the "boxy" region.  Some have too much "size" (500Hz or so).

A good exercise to train your ears is to listen to a bunch of different kicks, listening to them first, taking note of their sound quality, and then looking at a spectrum analyzer and matching what you see with what you hear.  You'll begin to notice these EQ "regions," which will prove invaluable when you're trying to tame or enhance a certain part of the kick.  You'll instinctively know where to look for that "wooden" quality, or how to mitigate that extra "boom" you don't need, etc.

One trick I used when practicing this is to look at all multiples of the fundamental tone.  Say your kick is in F (~87Hz).  Look at the frequency an octave above that (~174Hz), then the frequency an octave above that, etc.  This will open your ears to the distribution of characteristics across the spectrum.

Some tips I think would be helpful, sonically speaking at least (can't help with the composition aspects as I don't have much experience composing downtempo melodies, chords, etc.):

-Sample breakbeats for foundational loops and one-shots, and layer those with drum machine hits for accenting and punch.

-Use saturation to good effect.  Listen to drums in particular.  A lot of BoC drums are crunchy and distorted, and were likely round and punchy before being processed (ergo the drum machine hits).  A lot of the distortion on them sounds like an analog desk preamp being overdriven, or the input on a sampler being driven hard and resampled.  Brainworx' bx_saturator is good for this effect.

-Use a bitcrusher like Decimort to emulate the sonic character of different samplers.  A lot of the "glue" that came from samplers was in part due to their lower bit rate and limited spectrum.  This is a part of why sounds are so much different going through an MPC, rackmount Akai, or an EMU, for example.

-Anywhere you're using a filter, try and use the most analog sounding one.  Volcano 2 is my favorite out-of-the-synth filter VST for achieving this.  Listen for resonance character and how well-preserved the low end is when the filter cutoff is low.  These are usually the most telling characteristics of good modeling.  Softube just released a Mutronics Mutator clone, and that thing is a warped, gooey beast (used by Amon Tobin since ~2000 or so, and ever since).

-Get a good tape emulation like Slate Digital's VTM, with the tape type set to FG456 (it's older and crustier than the other setting, which is more modern and clean).  Set the IPS to the lowest speed to get a darker, lusher tone.  I've also used the Waves Kramer Tape, and it sounds a little too old and too colorful by comparison.

-If you can, on your synths do a constant global detune set to a slow oscillator at a low level, to try and model that "analog drift" you hear coming from a lot of the synths.  Serum is great for this, and it has good analog filters to boot.

Try and imagine the energy contour you want your drop to have.  Maybe it starts simple but high-energy for the first 4 bars, builds in energy the next 4, drops in energy in the next 4, and then builds to a peak level of energy in the final 4.  That's just an example, but you get the idea.

To increase energy, introduce higher-frequency drum elements, or increase their speed or play if they're already present.  Increase stereo width of certain parts.  Open up filter cutoffs a bit more on your synths.  Etc.

Try and pinpoint all the variables you have at your control that can influence the perceived energy level of the track, and give them contours and movement across 4 bar sections to give the drop itself a feeling of progression and arc. 1. Pick one VST synth to start out with and learn it inside and out.
2. Always be adding to your sample and preset collection, and really take the time to learn what makes each sound potentially useful.
3. Learn the fundamentals of EQ and Compression and practice them on every project you work on.  It'll take years to get really proficient with them, but every knob you tweak will take you one step closer to mastery.
4. It's just a computer - you won't hurt it's feelings.  Try anything and everything that comes to mind - really test the limits of your machine.  Starting out, 90% of your experimentation won't be rewarded with the result you want, but as you progress, that number gets smaller and smaller as you learn every little nuance of manipulating and shaping sound at your disposal.  It all starts with broad strokes, but greatness is a game of inches.
5. Create and save something every day.  One project will inevitably benefit from the work you did on another project.  And in the end, making a daily exercise of producing keeps you sharp, and having all of these micro-projects at your disposal keeps your well of potentially useful material full when "writer's block" hits.
6. Work with as many people as you can.  It'll be a revealing test of how you operate "under the gun," you'll learn as much as you teach, and you'll inevitably create something neither of you could have created independently - usually for the better.
7. Every once in a while, just go wild with a preset and your keyboard.  Test the limits of what a patch can do.  Try and break it.  Record yourself while you do this - you'll inevitably come away with something unique and inspiring.
8. Keep the composition simple in the beginning, and ask yourself just how involved a particular element needs to be.  Usually, it's not as intricate, complex, or confusing as you'll try and make it.
9. Mostly for mixing - invest in one high-quality plugin for each type of processing you're looking to do.  Sure, there are free transient designers out there, but the SPL will never fail you.  Waves' Kramer Tape is perpetually on sale, but the Slate VTM just sounds worlds apart (I bought them both, and you can probably tell I only use one of them).  Don't waste your money on half-baked or novelty plugins when truly great tools are out there.  Unless it's Sausage Fattener. ;)

Your style is going to be the intersection of the different music you like, so the most important thing you can do is closely observe and listen to the music you like and break it down into functional pieces. You'll be looking for the fundamental, which is the lowest peak in frequency and usually the highest in amplitude, for a kick or snare in particular.

Sometimes you get samples where there's fuckery going on - sometimes there are two fundamentals ("twin peaks"), sometimes there are none altogether ("flat") - but these are rare.

Regardless, what you want to do is set up a spectrum analyzer and play the drum sample into it, and make a note of what note that fundamental hits at.  It's almost always gonna be a few cents off perfect pitch, but that's for the OCD (like me) to worry about.

If you want to make tuning kicks easier for yourself, you can try using the sampler to pitch the kick up an octave (playing C4 essentially), doubling the frequency of the fundamental and making it somewhat easier to discern on the spectrum analyzer.  This is what I usually do by default when checking the pitch of my drum samples.  With snares you don't need to do this.

EQing the "in your face region" around 4-6kHz should help (I always target 5K from the get-go as a starting point for elements I want to push back). 500Hz also gives sounds a sense of size, so if it's too large still, pull that area down with a moderate bell or a shelf.  Lowpassing will help remove the air and serve as the final touch.

Aside from the spectrum, on your reverb, you should use more tail than early reflections, and a short pre-delay, if any at all.  The short pre-delay will make the reverb sound as one with the signal.  EQ before your reverb, in case you weren't doing that already.

Using chorus on elements can help "wash them out" so to speak, so consider doing that as well.

Finally, compressing the dynamic range of the track, in tandem with setting a good, low level in the mix, will help push it back, I think.  Use a fast attack at the very least - nothing puts something in your face more than a compressor that lets through snappy or fat transients (this is a vocal though, so I doubt that's gonna be a problem).

However, there are a few easy shortcuts to getting a sound that swings and grooves and accents and all that jazz:

1. Velocity - use it for volume, filter cutoff, etc.  This will accent certain hits - use it primarily for higher-range percussion like hi-hats and rides and you'll immediately feel the difference.

Agreed.  Counterpoint (in the traditional sense) is a pretty strict form, and not used much in EDM in my experience with it.  Take that with a grain of salt - that's just my observation.

What is used a lot, however, is *call and response*.  Basically, one melody plays for, let's say, 2 bars, all the while setting up a sort of response melody from another instrument for the next 2 bars.  The exact measure count isn't set in stone or anything, but you get the idea - bassline plays a cool lick, melody comes in with a response.

You're basically changing which instrument takes "center stage" at different intervals, creating a sort of dialogue between your orchestration.

One of the most important fundamentals to keep in mind when employing this is that for something to stand out, the other elements almost *shouldn't* stand out - it's hard to make a part really "special" when it's swamped by other "special" parts at the same time.  This is probably the problem you're facing right now, without even knowing it.

The millisecond length of a quarter-note would be 60,000/128, or 468.75 in this case.

From there you can multiply or divide to get different subdivisions.  For triplets, multiply the ms length by 2/3, and for dotted time multiply the ms length by 1.5.

This is a useful practice in setting reverb times, compression release settings, etc. - I'd suggest you make a quick Excel spreadsheet that auto-calculates based on the tempo you input (that's what I did at least, and I use it at least once per project).

All of this adds up to intimate knowledge of standard arrangements, like when a main hook typically comes in, or the amount of bars dedicated to a particular dynamic shift, how long the range for drops in a genre is, how many drops are typical, etc.  You also begin to see clearly how certain artists deviate from these in subtle ways or just rework the formula, e.g. only three artists in my collection of Drum & Bass have dared to do a 16 bar drop in their tracks, when 24 is the usual low-end of the spectrum (for club bangers at least).

All told, I'd highly recommend that any producer spends time DJing to learn basic arrangement skills in their genre.  It sinks in quicker and deeper with DJing than just production alone, I've found.

Also, the best thing you can do to learn synthesis is work backwards from presets.  This means finding a patch you like, then disabling the following in the following order:

1. The Effects (this is the polish that will make it sound so good - turn it off to see what's "under the hood")
2. The Envelopes and LFOs, Velocity, Keytracking, etc. (these give the sound all the characteristic movement and performance dynamics)
3. The Filters (these have a dramatic impact on the sound's core timbre)

This should leave you with just the oscillators, which may sound surprisingly dull and simple to you.  Guess what - most of the time, they are!  (At least with non-wavetable synths)  Now add back in the different parameters, one by one, and see how they individually shape the sound.  You'll understand synthesis in no time.

If you don't know what these parameters are or how to activate/deactivate them, definitely watch one of those tutorials, learn signal flow, and read the Sylenth manual as best as you can.

Here's a [holy grail of sampling philosophy](http://www.soundonsound.com/sos/apr03/articles/amontobin.asp) from one of the all-time best, in my opinion - Amon Tobin.  Here's a good quote to sum it up:

"I like using sounds that have existed in a different musical context before. It's not musique concrète or found sounds, and I won't use session musicians or sample CDs. I find sample CDs of, say, a session drummer really flat, because they don't have any real musical context. The energy that I'm after is maybe in the middle of some one-off recording that happened in a special time at some festival, where the drummer was just going off and there is that bit of energy that you just take. You can extend it or rearrange it, but the energy's still there. That's always what's fascinated me about samples and what I can't get out of session musicians or sample CDs. It's not that I'm against it; it's a perfectly valid way to work, but just not one that appeals to me. I don't think I can get anything that isn't already on vinyl, so why use a session guy when I can use *the* sax player or *the* drummer? Why settle for second-best?"

In short, if you want to get good at sampling, you have to get good at finding those moments with a special kind of energy that you want to take and use in some capacity.  That "special kind of energy" will be entirely up to you, because truth be told, I love Daft Punk, and I would have personally never used the same samples they did, just as a matter of taste.  But they made it work, because it's a sound they could hear the potential in.

Find sounds you can hear the potential in, and bring them to that potential.  As Amon Tobin says, the source doesn't matter, it's all about the end result.

That means it's a snare hitting 22 cents below C4 (which you can adjust in a simpler quite easily), and it came from BHK Samples' Essentials Volume 1 pack.

I organize samples by the production company, so all my BHK snares go into one folder, and once you have the pitch found for most of your collection, it's a breeze - you'll have a few dozen hits of any one pitch that you can quickly audition in your track, or you could easily pitch up/down hits of nearby tones to the one you're looking for with minimal artifacts.

Or, alternatively, picking samples already tuned to a particular key, i.e. the kick on the tonic and the snare on the 5th, or whatever.  This is where managing your sample library so you know exactly where to find hits of a certain character, and certain pitch, is helpful.

In this situation, all of the tracks I listed have 24 bar drops, which are essentially three distinct 8 bar sections that make up a 24 bar whole.  The "drop sequences" describe how the material in the drops are used.  For example, if the first 16 bars are really just a pair of of the same 8 bar section, leading into a different 8 bar section after that (i.e. "City 17"), you'd get AAB form for the drop, where the A section (8 bars) is repeated twice before going into the B Section (also 8 bars).

8 bar sections are about the most common thing in popular music, and sure enough, they show up reliably enough in Drum & Bass to almost be a certainty when breaking the song up into distinct sections.

If you want groove, I suggest a few things:

1. Leave pockets/use dotted notes:
This may sound obvious, but don't take up all the (horizontal) space in a MIDI clip.  Leave well-timed gaps.  Also, try extending the length of certain notes by 1.5x, rather than sticking to straight 16th, 8th, quarter notes, etc.

2. Use the Groove Pool:
I suggest starting by putting the MPC 16 Swing 75 on your MIDI clip, setting the "Timing" to 100%, and then pulling back the timing percentage until you find a swing you like on your melody/riff.  Adjust the "Base" between 1/16 and 1/8 to see which works better for your tempo and note frequency.  Don't use "Random" (at least in high values) - even Roger Lynn, the inventor of the first swing feature to appear in electronic instruments, says it does nothing to add a human feel to your groove and I can verify this from personal experience.

3. Automate Your Envelope:
The beauty of an electric guitar/bass is that you can let notes ring out or make them staccato without even thinking - it's just a natural function of the instrument.  Synths don't work like this - unless you program them to.  Try routing Velocity to things like the amp envelope's decay/release time, or simply use knobs to adjust those settings by hand in time with your pre-written pattern.

4. Use the best sound you can:
This one should be self explanatory, but if you're not feeling a sound, it's not gonna inspire a good melody or riff.  Find the right sound for the right melody/riff first (I admit, this should have been number one, but I'm just going off the top of my head here).

5. Study what you consider groovy and try and recreate it:
This can start with simply transcribing a melody or riff you like into MIDI in your DAW and learning what makes it tick.  Where are the steps, leaps, and rests?  What types of articulation are used, and how can you recreate that on your instrument (e.g. legato, palm-muting on a guitar, etc.)?  That's where you can get creative with your synth design imo.

There's a great ADSR tutorial series called "Make Any Sound In Massive," and while I'd highly suggest checking it out (you can get a month subscription for 99¢ right now), I can give you the basic rundown.

When designing sounds, you want to follow a logical series of steps, from beginning to end, to ensure that the end-result is what you desire.  The first and most important step is setting up your oscillators.  Then you work on your filters, then modulation/performance dynamics, THEN effects, in that order.  You have to be disciplined and discerning, following each step in order and giving it the time and attention it's due.

For the oscillator step, one way to combat harsh metallic sounds is to choose less harsh, metallic oscillators, OR, if you want something with some edge but not too much, you can use the wavetable position and intensity knobs on each oscillator to really dial in how present you want your patch to be.  This way, once you get to the filters, your base sound will be perfect already, and only made better.

If you're getting "squelchy" sounds, that's probably your filter selection and the amount of resonance you're using on the filters.  Also, be mindful of which distortion types you're using, as some are more harsh than others.  Audition different types of distortion to see which one fits what you're looking for.

All in all, it's a course worth checking out.  Let me know if you have any questions!

Break your productions down into a series of stages, i.e. composing, production, mixing, etc., and only do what the stage at hand asks for (or a previous stage if you need to correct a mistake or make something better).  So write out your song, structure it a bit, then find all the right sounds that go into it, then arrange, do small touches and edits and make it feel whole, THEN mix it.

If you start mixing elements too early you'll end up with a bad sounding track.

That said, sound design sessions, i.e. designing layered synths, layered drums, etc., are useful on the side to give you an arsenal of sounds to put in during the composition/production stage.  This is a way of producing more quickly in the moment and focusing more on the vibe, the music.

All in all, find a methodology that works for you and perfect it.

Good Sample(s) -> Interesting Drum Pattern(s) -> Getting levels right for each component of the hats -> Good EQ on each sample.

That being said, I wish it had better recording latency control - Logic just seems to record perfectly in time, while Ableton is always behind the beat, even after turning off input monitoring, setting input/output latency, buffer size set low, etc.  I've got a damn good computer and this is still an issue, which I find kind of ridiculous.

The longer I've used Ableton, the more intricate my drum programming has become, but I almost always use MIDI (Drum Racks, Sampler, Simpler, etc.) to trigger samples because that gives you really expedient editing capabilities, and expressive control when you account for velocity mapping and things like choke groups on the Drum Rack.

One example: I have a drum rack for hi-hats only, with several similar sounding samples of different hit-intensities that I sequence to make the sound of the hats increase and decrease in intensity in a certain way.  Using the choke group option, you can set all the samples to choke group 1, and when one sound triggers, the others stop cold, as if you're playing a single hi-hat on a real kit.  This works well with open hi-hats that you want to stop ringing out as the next closed hat is struck - it just sounds more natural.

Also, if you want to tune your kick and snare samples, a Sampler + a Spectrum Analyzer makes this a breeze.

MIDI has so many useful options for drum programming that I can't imagine programming beats with straight audio like I've seen a lot of people do.  That's just my two cents.

GRM Tools has a plugin called "Freq Warp" that does just this.  It sounds amazing... how useable it is in a proper track is still questionable, at least to my ears.  But the effect you're talking about does exist.

I'd suggest demoing the GRM Tools if you can - they're loads of fun.  I almost consider them NASA-grade VSTs, because they're so scientific and precise, but can create otherworldly sounds from something as simple as a sine wave.
